fig1_macrostate_distribution.svg: Macrostate distribution of a fair two-state system from two_state_probability$(N,n)=\binom{N}{n}/2^N$, shown as a density in the fraction $x=n/N$ for $N=16,64,256$ (dots), with the de Moivre-Laplace Gaussian gaussian_approx_two_state (lines) tracking it. As $N$ grows the peak at $x=\tfrac12$ grows taller and narrower — collapsing toward a delta function — the microscopic root of a sharp thermodynamic limit.
fig2_fractional_width.svg: Relative fluctuation of the two-state macrostate from fractional_width: $\sigma/\langle n\rangle=1/\sqrt{N}$, a line of slope $-\tfrac12$ on log-log axes. It is $10\%$ at $N=10^2$ but only $\sim3\times10^{-12}$ at $N\sim10^{23}$ — at macroscopic particle number the macrostate is effectively certain, which is exactly why thermodynamics looks deterministic.
